summary.text: A 31-year-old man on an all-oral longer regimen for pulmonary MDR-TB, in its initial phase for 25 days, was brought to the outpatient department with irrelevant talk, violent behavior, loss of sleep and headache for five days. He had been treated for drug-sensitive extra-pulmonary TB one year earlier and had no history of psychiatric disorder or substance abuse.

Examination showed increased psychomotor activity, elevated mood, anxiety and pressured speech with a Young Mania Rating Scale score of 19 and Brief Psychosis Rating Score of 36. Laboratory tests, CSF studies with negative treponemal tests, and a head CT within normal limits were obtained, and a provisional diagnosis of drug-induced psychosis was made after meningitis, neurosyphilis and other differentials were ruled out.

The MDR-TB drugs were put on hold and he was admitted and given lorazepam, promethazine, haloperidol, nitrazepam, olanzapine and thiamine, improving by the third day post-admission. After antipsychotics were discontinued, drugs were rechallenged from the eighth day, and cycloserine was followed by a relapse of symptoms; all drugs were stopped again.

He returned to normalcy on the third day and a final diagnosis of cycloserine-induced psychosis was made. The regimen was modified by omitting cycloserine and adding ethionamide, with no further episodes of psychosis or insomnia. He was discharged after one week of initiating ethionamide, with advice for follow-up for 18 months.
